newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean non-life insurers see profits plunge.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean non-life insurers see profits plunge.

text.p: South Korea's non-life insurance firms saw profits plunge in the year to March, eroded by growing competition in underwriting and soaring operating expenses, analysts said on Thursday.
Moreover, their profits are expected to deteriorate in the current year as claims continue to rise sharply and the growth potential of premium income is limited, they said.
"Fast-growing expenses were and will be the top factor depressing their profits," said Lee Hwa-yeol, an analyst at Ssangyong Investment and Securities.
"Companies are spending more and more on sales people and in providing various gifts such as free gasoline tickets to attract more clients," he said.

In the year to March after-tax net profits of the 17 non-life insurance firms in South Korea fell to a combined 56.16 billion won ($63.21 million) from 132.74 billion a year earlier, the Korea Non-life Insurance Association said.
Their underwriting losses widened by 46.4 percent to a combined 1.01 trillion won while premium income grew by a slower 21.3 percent to 14.4 trillion won, the association said.

"Underwriting losses are widening because companies feel limits in raising their premium rates as the underwriting competition keeps heating up," said Lee Ki-hyung, an analyst at the Korea Insurance Development Institute.
Net operating expenses during the year increased by 44.9 percent to 3.39 trillion won from 2.34 trillion won a year earlier, the association said.
Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance Co remained the largest of the nation's 11 non-life insurers with a 24.2 percent share in terms of premium income.
The 11 firms exclude credit guarantee insurance firms, a reinsurance firm and three small foreign firms operating in South Korea.

Samsung's premium income more than doubled to 3.07 trillion won in the year to March 1997 from 1.46 trillion won a year earlier, but its net profit rose only slightly to 12.36 billion won from 12.13 billion.
Next came Hyundai Marine and Fire Insurance Co and Dongbu Fire and Marine Insurance Co with premium income of 1.8 trillion and 1.75 trillion won, respectively.
Hyundai's net profit fell to 6.02 billion won from 7.02 billion and Dongbu's to 57.6 billion won from 101.84 billion.
Dongbu's net profit fell sharply because the previous year's profit was distorted by a 59.1 billion won extraordinary gain recorded during the year to March 1996, analysts said.
Haedong Fire & Marine Insurance Co was the only firm to record a loss during the year. It ran a net loss of 19.25 billion won, compared with a 3.19 billion won net profit in the previous year.
Analysts attributed the company's red ink to a relatively heavy proportion of premium income from automobile insurance policies in the company's total income.
"Underwriting competition is most severe in the automobile insurance market and therefore, profitability in the sector is worsening every year," said Lee of Ssangyong.
